column6: The commentary presents the Lord as the one who brings forth pasture for herds; creation assigns every beast the green plant for food, placing animal grazing within God’s original provision.

column5: Moses as a shepherd before his mission
column6: The commentary points to Moses’ answer to Pharaoh as its explicit grazing scene; Exodus first shows Moses shepherding Jethro’s flock and bringing it to Horeb, giving that speaker a prior pastoral setting without retelling the Pharaoh encounter.

column5: Moses’ compassion for a stray lamb
column6: The commentary says a shepherd surrounds and protects animals and compares this to a ruler’s care of subjects; this midrash says Moses was chosen after he carried a tired lamb to water, interpreting leadership as attentive care for the vulnerable.

column5: A shepherd protects his flock from predators
column6: The commentary defines the shepherd as protecting livestock; David recounts pursuing a lion or bear that took a lamb from the flock, giving a concrete human example of pastoral guardianship.

column5: Rescuing the lamb from the predator
column6: The commentary’s shepherd preserves the herd; David says he struck the predator and rescued the lamb from its mouth, specifying protection as active recovery.

column5: Shepherd and ruler are one role
column6: The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Israel’s elders tell David that he will shepherd Israel and be its leader, explicitly joining pastoral care and political rule.

column5: Moses leads Israel like a flock
column6: The commentary points to Moses’ pastoral reply to Pharaoh and develops guidance of a herd; the psalm recalls God leading his people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, placing the image in the Exodus story.

The commentary links the shepherd of animals to the ruler of people; God takes David from following nursing ewes to shepherd Jacob, making the transition from literal flock care to leadership explicit.
The commentary’s flock leaders guide those behind them and its ruler tends subjects; David shepherds Israel with an upright heart and guides them with skillful hands, uniting care and guidance.

column5: Know the state of the flock
column6: The commentary describes a shepherd who watches where matters will lead and a ruler who tends subjects; this proverb tells the keeper to know the condition of his flocks and attend to his herds, turning oversight into concrete attention.

column5: Stars counted and called by God
column6: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch includes watching the stars and connects oversight with knowing an outcome; Isaiah asks the reader to look at the created host, which God brings out by number and calls by name, relocating cosmic knowledge in the Creator.
The commentary extends shepherding to rulers over people; Isaiah calls Cyrus God’s shepherd, who will carry out the rebuilding of Jerusalem, giving the political metaphor a foreign royal instance.

column5: Moses leads God’s flock through the sea
column6: The commentary invokes Moses speaking of grazing to Pharaoh; Isaiah recalls the one who brought Moses and God’s flock up from the sea, connecting the named speaker with God’s shepherding in the Exodus deliverance.

The commentary says rulers shepherd their subjects and the herd’s leaders guide others; God promises shepherds who will feed the people with knowledge and understanding, specifying instruction as a form of guidance.

The commentary’s herd leaders are those who guide others; Jeremiah describes lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray in the mountains, showing the same leadership relation reversed into misguidance.
The commentary’s shepherd protects and watches over the herd; Ezekiel’s sheep wander across mountains and hills with no one searching for them, portraying the result when pastoral oversight fails.
The commentary pairs a protected pasture with a shepherd who guards it; Ezekiel asks why well-fed sheep trample the rest of the pasture, making care for shared grazing land part of the pastoral duty.
The commentary’s pasture is a provision belonging to the flock; Ezekiel says God’s sheep must eat what the strong sheep have trampled, adding harm within the flock to the image.
The commentary makes the owner, the flock, and its guide parts of one scene; God promises one shepherd, his servant David, over the sheep, linking divine ownership with a human ruler’s care.

The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Micah’s ruler stands and shepherds his flock in YHWH’s strength, after which the people dwell securely, joining leadership, divine backing, and protection.

column5: Stars as a sign of future outcome
column6: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch connects watching stars with seeing where an affair will end; God brings Abram outside to look at the stars as a sign of his future descendants, a related but distinct use of the heavens to frame what is to come.

column5: Watching stars and refusing their worship
column6: The commentary mentions star-watching as a secondary r-ʿ-y sense while assigning the ultimate oversight to the Lord; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to be drawn into bowing to the sun, moon, and stars, adding a caution about confusing observation with divine rule.

The commentary connects pasture brought forth by God with grazing animals; Isaiah promises rain for seed and fodder for livestock, then says the land’s produce will be rich, joining animal provision to the land’s yield.

The commentary says pasture is turned into waste; Joel depicts cattle groaning and herds wandering because there is no pasture, showing the consequence for dependent animals when grazing land is lost.

column5: Peter told to shepherd Jesus’ sheep
column6: The commentary extends the shepherd’s care to a ruler’s subjects; the risen Jesus tells Peter to shepherd his sheep, transferring pastoral responsibility to a human leader.
The commentary’s shepherd protects and tends livestock; Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep, specifying practical provision as part of the leadership charge.
The commentary says a governor shepherds his subjects; Paul charges overseers to shepherd God’s church, which God acquired, making pastoral leadership both delegated and accountable.

The commentary describes the shepherd as one who watches over and protects a flock; Peter says the addressees returned from straying like sheep to the shepherd and guardian of their souls, applying the image to spiritual oversight.

The commentary compares a ruler’s care for subjects with a shepherd’s care for livestock; Peter tells elders not to dominate those entrusted to them but to be examples, adding an ethical limit to pastoral authority.

column5: The great shepherd of the sheep
column6: The commentary’s Rab is owner and shepherd of the flock; Hebrews calls Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep, grounding pastoral leadership in God’s covenant and the raising of Jesus from the dead.

The commentary says a ruler shepherds his subjects; Revelation depicts the child destined to shepherd all nations with an iron rod, preserving the political shepherd image while giving it a forceful judgment register.
